html:
In the 1640s planters on Barbados switched from tobacco to sugar, learning methods used in Dutch Brazil. Within a generation the island was covered in cane fields, mills and boiling houses.

Sugar needed huge labour, and the planters turned to enslaved Africans bought through the Atlantic slave trade. By the 1660s Africans were the majority, and Barbados was the richest colony England had.

Big estates swallowed the small farms, and many poor whites left. The Barbados model of large plantations, enslaved majorities and harsh laws, written down in the Slave Code of 1661, was copied across the West Indies and the American South. It made sugar, and rum from its molasses, the great Atlantic trade.
